# Introduction 

## Source
- Health Verity (HV)
- U.S. Postal Service
- U.S. Census Bureau 
- National Weather Service 
- American Community Survey 
- the IRS
- NASA/Columbia University

## Data
Health determinants of Americans who got or did not get a timely diagnosis for metastatic triple negative breast cancers (within 90 days) 

- e.g. race, location, education level of location, income of location, diagnosed within 90 days

\textbf{Note:} Getting a timely diagnosis is good indicator for healthcare access

## Goal
\textbf{Observe any health disparities associated with patient race and/or other factors}


```{r}
data = df , family = binomial
```

## Coefficient Plots: Log Odds Scale
```{r, include = TRUE}
# Plot on log odds scale
signif_coefs <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(glm.fits)))
signif_coefs <- subset(signif_coefs, signif_coefs[, 4] < 0.05)
signif_coefs$Predictor <- rownames(signif_coefs)
ggplot((signif_coefs), aes(x = Predictor, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Coefficient Plot (Log Odds Scale)", y = "Coefficient", x = "Predictors")

```

## Coefficient Plots: Odds scale
```{r}
# Plot on odds scale
signif_coefs_odds <- signif_coefs
signif_coefs_odds$Estimate <- exp(signif_coefs$Estimate)
ggplot(signif_coefs_odds, aes(x = Predictor, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Coefficient Plot (Odds Scale)", y = "Coefficient", x = "Predictors")
```

## Coefficient Plots: Summary
Using $\alpha$ = 0.05, and if logistic regression model is good model for our data...

### Strongest determinants of receiving a timely diagnosis:
- `education_bachelors`
- `education_less_highschool`
- `education_highschool`
- `education_some_college`

### `hispanic` and `patient_raceWhite`
- `hispanic`: magnitude is very small and can be treated as zero

- `patient_raceWhite`: positive coefficient magnitude 

## Coefficient Plots: Summary

### `payer_type`, `family_size`, `DivisionEast South Central`    
- All negative coefficient 
- `payer_type`: 
    + All same coefficient magnitudes
    
        + Meaning all same predictive access to healthcare
          
    + Known `payer_type` being compared to unknown/blank `payer_type` 
    
    + Therefore, we cannot make any meaningful inference

### `income_household_75_to_100`, `DivisionMountain`
- All positive coefficient 


## Using Predicted Probabilities to Predict Response Values
```{r, include = TRUE}
##Generate Predicted Probabilities
glm.probs <- predict(glm.fits, type = "response")

glm.pred <- rep(0, 12873)
glm.pred[glm.probs > .5] = 1

attach(df)
##confusion matrix
cm <- table(glm.pred, y)

sensitivity <- (cm[2,2])/sum(cm[,2])
specificity <- cm[1,1]/sum(cm[,1])

##has to match y level: training error rate  
training_error_rate <- mean(as.factor(glm.pred) == y) 

initial.pred <- data.frame(training_error_rate, specificity, sensitivity)
initial.pred

```
### Training Error Rate
Using the same data to fit the model, logistic regression made incorrect predictions 62.5% of the time.

### Training Specificity
Out of those who did not get a diagnosis, logistic regression correctly predicted 3.97% of the time. 

### Training Sensitivity
Out of those who did get a diagnosis, logistic regression correctly predicted 97.69% of the time.

## Cross-Validated Error Rates 
```{r}
storage <- as.data.frame(matrix(nrow = 10, ncol = 3))
n <- 12873
idx <- sample(n)
fold_size <- floor(n / 10)
for (i in 1:10) {
  # start and end positions of index vector for ith fold
  start_position <- (i - 1) * fold_size + 1
  end_position <- i * fold_size
  if (i == 10) {
    end_position <- n
  }
  # test indices (indices for ith fold)
  test_ind <- idx[start_position:end_position]
  
  # training indices (all indices not in ith fold)
  train_ind <- (1:n)[-test_ind]
  
  # fit model on all data except ith fold
  glm.fit_Train <- glm(y ~ ., data = df, subset = train_ind, family = binomial)
  
  # predict on ith fold
  pi_hat <- predict(glm.fit_Train, df[test_ind, ], type = "response")
  y_hat <- as.numeric(pi_hat > 0.5)
  
  # compute accuracy rates
  cmat <- table("Truth" = df[test_ind, "y"],
                "Pred" = y_hat)
  acc <- c("Overall" = sum(diag(cmat)) / sum(cmat), # Overall accuracy
           "Specificity" = cmat[1, 1] / sum(cmat[1, ]), # Specificity
           "Sensitivity" = cmat[2, 2] / sum(cmat[2, ])  # Sensitivity
  )
  storage[i, ] <- round(acc, 3)
  
}
names(storage) <- c("Overall Accuracy", "Specificity", "Sensitivity")

##average overall accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity 
cv_acc <- colMeans(storage)
names(cv_acc) <- c("Overall", "Specificity", "Sensitivity")

```

### Testing Accuracy, Specificity, and Sensitivity 
```{r, include = TRUE}
as.data.frame(t(cv_acc))

```

# Conclusion 

## Logistic Regression As Good As Null Classifier
It seems like logistic regression is just always predicting the response variable to be 1, or always predicting that people will receive the diagnosis within 90 days. 

- Predictive accuracy of our logistic regression model is as good as a blind/null classifier. 
 
 + Therefore, we do not consider the coefficients of the model.

### Next Step? 
- Better models?

    - Tree based method (random forest)

    - Machine learning model 

- Or maybe there is just no meaningful relationships between predictors and response variable?
